\subsection{The band a distortion budget works in}
\label{sec:operating}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/saturation_RECIPE512.png}
\caption{\textbf{Three regions, and only the middle one is a design choice.}
Below the floor no allocation meets the budget; above saturation every tile
already takes the cheapest exit. The $0.1\dB$ budget uses \BandUseLow\% of the
band at the lowest rate and \BandUseHigh\% at the highest.}
\label{fig:operating}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/operating}}
\caption{\textbf{Floor and saturation}, dB below the released decoder. The floor
is what tiling costs with no early exit at all; saturation is where every tile
reaches exit $j$ and the ceiling of Eq.~(\ref{eq:ceiling}) is reached.}
\label{tab:operating}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/theory.png}
\caption{\textbf{The structure of the allocation}, on one frame. \textbf{a}, compute and
distortion are monotone in the multiplier. \textbf{b}, the frontier, with both ends
and both dead bands marked on the panel. \textbf{c}, what the
Lagrangian reaches against the exact Pareto set, enumerated by dynamic
programming.}
\label{fig:theory}
\end{figure}

The construction has enough structure to state as propositions, and we check each
One assumption is worth naming before any of this. The argument treats the
frame's distortion as a sum over tiles, while the deblocking pass runs on the
stitched frame and therefore sees the whole exit map at once, so the tiles are
not strictly independent. We measured the size of that coupling over $60$
allocations and the largest mismatch between the separable prediction and a real
decode is $5.5\times10^{-5}\dB$, four orders of magnitude below the budget. We
proceed as if the objective were separable and treat that as measured rather
than assumed.

We check each
one numerically instead of asserting it (\texttt{scripts/verify\_theory.py},
seven of seven).

\begin{enumerate}\itemsep1pt
\item The allocation decouples per tile.
\item Compute is non-increasing and distortion non-decreasing in $\lambda$.
\item The sweep traces the lower convex hull, so it cannot reach an interior
      point of the achievable set.
\item $\lambda{=}0$ reaches the least distortion the ladder can produce.
\item Beyond a finite $\lambda$, computable in closed form as
      $\max_t \max_k (D_{t,j}-D_{t,k})/(c_k-c_j)$, the allocation is the
      constant map to exit $j$, at cost exactly $c_j$.
\item The ceiling is a function of the split depth alone.
\end{enumerate}

The third of those has a practical edge. The sweep reaches only hull vertices, so
a budget that falls between two of them cannot be met exactly. We measured what
that costs by enumerating the \emph{exact} Pareto set with dynamic programming
over tiles, which is feasible because there are only four distinct exit costs. The
sweep reaches 95 allocations against a Pareto set of 635, and the loss from
convexity is at most $0.05$ saving points (Fig.~\ref{fig:theory}c). For this
problem the standard construction is essentially optimal.

It matters \emph{why} that loss is small, since the reason is structural and
points at what would make it smaller. The reachable costs form a lattice, and its
spacing is set by how much the mean cost moves when the multiplier crosses a
breakpoint. If $m$ tiles each move to the next exit there, the spacing is at most
$m\max_k(c_{k+1}-c_k)/N$ saving points. The convexity loss cannot exceed the
largest spacing, because a budget between two levels is served by the lower one.
Here $m{=}2$, since tiles with identical rows switch together, and the bound is
$0.745$ points; the measured spacing sits exactly on it. Nothing in the
expression depends on content or rate, and the bound falls as $1/N$: halving the
tile side puts four times as many tiles on the lattice, each carrying a quarter
of the step. Fine granularity is what makes the Lagrangian relaxation lossless in
practice, and no property of the images is doing that work.

Two numbers bound what any budget can do (Table~\ref{tab:operating}) and Fig.~\ref{fig:operating}. The
\textbf{floor} $D_{\min}$ is the distortion of a tiled decode with every tile at
full depth, which is pure tiling penalty: \FloorLow$\dB$ at $q0$, rising to
\FloorHigh$\dB$ at $q63$. A budget below it admits no allocation. The
\textbf{saturation} point $D_{\mathrm{sat}}$ is the distortion when every tile
takes exit $j$; any budget at or above it reaches $S_{\max}$, and a larger one
reaches nothing more.

One consequence of that is worth stating plainly. At $q0$ the ceiling is reached
at \SatLow$\dB$, so the architectural bound behaves as an operating point rather
than as an asymptote. Past it, the limiting factor is the \emph{ladder} and not
the budget, which is an argument for a finer ladder before a looser budget. The
same two numbers pick out a narrow regime: budgets in
$[\SatLow, \SatWindowHi)\dB$ saturate the lowest rate and nothing else, a range
\SatWindowMb\ thousandths of a decibel wide.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/budget_band.png}
\caption{\textbf{The band is the rate dependence.} \textbf{a} Saving against the
budget, with each rate's floor and saturation point ticked. \textbf{b} The same
with the budget axis rescaled onto each rate's own band. Five curves become one; dashed is the one-parameter power law
fitted to all of them.}
\label{fig:band}
\end{figure}

\textbf{And the band is almost all of the rate dependence.} At a matched
decibel the five rates are \BandRawSpread\ points apart. Rescale the budget axis
onto each rate's own band, with the floor at $0$ and saturation at $1$, and they
collapse onto a single master curve, \BandSpreadMean\ points apart on average and
\BandSpreadMax\ at worst (Fig.~\ref{fig:band}). The answer to ``how much does a
$0.1\dB$ budget buy at this rate'' is therefore, to within a couple of points,
``where does $0.1\dB$ sit in this rate's band''. The floor and the saturation
point are both in closed form and both cheap to measure. What they leave over is
small enough that a deployment could calibrate the two ends and read the rest off
one curve. That curve is a one-parameter power law,
$\text{saving} \approx C\,u^{\BandExp}$, with $C$ the architectural ceiling and
$u$ the position in the band. We fit it in log space over all five rates and get
$R^2 = \BandRTwo$, worst residual \BandFitErr\ points. The claim we make is the
\emph{rescaling}: measuring the budget in units of each rate's own band is what
collapses the curves. The exponent is an empirical fit to that collapse and not
a law. Inverse fits to the same frontier disagree in it by up to $40\%$, so we
report it as a description of these curves and read nothing into its value.

\textbf{The collapse appears robust across two checkpoints.} We repeated the
measurement on a different training run, \texttt{BEST}, a separate recipe taken
at a different epoch, and the same thing happens. The rates are
\BandRawSpreadB\ points apart at a matched decibel and \BandSpreadMeanB\ after
rescaling, and the collapsed curve is again a power law, $R^2 = \BandRTwoB$. The
\emph{exponent} does not carry over: \BandExpB\ there against \BandExp\ here, so
it describes a trained decoder and not the architecture. What replicates is the
collapse. Within a checkpoint, the rate dependence of the trade-off is the rate
dependence of the band (Fig.~\ref{fig:tradeoff}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/tradeoff.png}
\caption{\textbf{The trade-off, whole.} \textbf{a} What a budget buys, per rate;
the dotted line is the arithmetic ceiling,
\CeilingModelled\%, and $q0$ reaches it at \SatLow\dB. \textbf{b} The
same relation inverted, so it reads as what a saving target costs. The three
budgets reported elsewhere are three points on this curve.}
\label{fig:tradeoff}
\end{figure}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/window.png}
\caption{\textbf{The window a budget works in.} \textbf{a}, saving against the distortion actually delivered, per rate. Every curve begins at a floor and flattens at a saturation point. \textbf{b}, those two limits against rate; the shaded band is the only region in which a budget is a design choice rather than a formality.}
\label{fig:window}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Signalled versus predicted allocation}
\label{sec:ab}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/router_ab.png}
\caption{\textbf{Who decides.} \textbf{(a)} The two decision paths of
Section~\ref{sec:setting}, drawn side by side: the encoder's search over all $K$
exits per tile against the head's forward pass over decoded data.
\textbf{(b)} Saving at 0.1\,dB; shading is what a bit-exact bitstream costs.
\textbf{(c)} That cost is smallest at $q\GapMinQp$, where the router needs
almost no cost multiplier to reach the budget from where it was trained, and
grows in both directions. At $0.3\dB$ it falls to the router's own
\RouterCostPct\,\% wherever the budget saturates the ladder, and widens where it
does not.}
\label{fig:ab}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/ab}}
\caption{\textbf{Signalled against predicted} at two budgets, same checkpoint and
test set, with one router trained against the oracle on the deployed table at a
single $\lambda$.}
\label{tab:ab}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:ab} compares the two, and what it prices is exactness against
bits (Fig.~\ref{fig:ab}). Panel~a puts the two decision paths side by side; the
only place they differ is who holds the source. A searches at the encoder, which
has the picture, and sends the answer; B guesses at the decoder, which has only
the latent.
\textbf{Not signalling costs \GapMin--\GapMax\ points}, roughly flat across
rate, for zero added bits and a byte-identical file. The gap is smallest at
$q\GapMinQp$ and widens toward both ends of the rate range.

\textbf{It tracks $|\beta|$}, the cost multiplier the bisection has to apply to
move a router trained at one $\lambda$ onto another operating point. At
$q\BetaMinQp$ the required $\beta$ is $\BetaAtMin$, essentially none, since
that is where the training $\lambda$ lands, and there the gap is at its minimum.
At $q0$ it is $\BetaLow$ and the gap is \GapMax. A large $\beta$ in either
direction lets the cost term dominate the logits, which discards the content
ranking the router learned. The remedy is a router per operating point, and a
deployment would have one anyway: a single set of weights covers all rates, and
a \RouterParams\ head per rate is $0.3\%$ of the model each.

Loosening the budget closes the gap only where the budget saturates the ladder.
At $0.3\dB$ the gap is \GapLooseLow\ points at the three lowest rates. That is
exactly the router's own \RouterCostPct\% of decode, so its \emph{prediction} is
free there; both configurations send every tile to the cheapest exit, and
nothing is left to predict wrongly. At the two highest rates $0.3\dB$ does not
saturate, and the gap \emph{widens} to \GapLooseHigh\ points. A looser budget
gives the allocation more room to be wrong in as well as more room to be right.

For a system that trains once, the single-router number is the honest one, so
that is what we report. It understates what B can do.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/beta_heldout}}
\caption{\textbf{Choosing $\beta$ without the test set.} Left, $\beta$ bisected
on the \HeldNCal\ held-out validation frames and then applied to the test frames
unchanged; right, $\beta$ bisected on the test frames themselves, which is what
Table~\ref{tab:ab} reports. Savings are hook counts on the routed decode with
the router's own compute charged against them. The last column re-bisects on the
test set to the quality the held-out $\beta$ delivered, so the two allocations
are differenced at one distortion rather than across two.}
\label{tab:betaheldout}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Where the $\beta$ above came from.} Every $\beta$ in
Table~\ref{tab:ab} was bisected against the budget on the test frames
themselves, which is the one thing Section~\ref{sec:alloc} says a decoder cannot
do. Table~\ref{tab:betaheldout} repeats the measurement with the table a
deployment would ship: $\beta$ bisected once per quality index on the \HeldNCal\
held-out Open Images validation frames, then applied to the CTC frames without
being touched again. Checkpoint, head, frames and budget are identical on both
sides, so what separates the two columns is where $\beta$ came from.

At $q0$ the two agree, \HeldBetaLow\ against \BetaLow\ and \HeldSavingLow\%
against \BLow\%, which is the same measurement to a hundredth of a point. At the
rates in between, the held-out $\beta$ misses the budget on the high side: it
delivers \HeldDbWorst\dB\ at $q\HeldDbWorstQp$ where $0.1\dB$ was asked for, and
\HeldNOver\ of the \HeldNHeld\ rates it covers overshoot. Distortion and saving
move together, so those rows also report more saving than Table~\ref{tab:ab}
does, and reading one column straight against the other would credit the router
with compute it bought using quality the budget did not allow. The last column
takes that back out, re-bisecting on the test set to the quality the held-out
$\beta$ actually delivered: at equal delivered quality the two allocations agree
to within \HeldTransferAbsMax\ points. What moves between the two sets is the
decibel a given $\beta$ delivers.

The highest rate fails harder than that. On the calibration frames the floor,
the distortion tiling costs with every tile already at the deepest exit, is
\HeldNoBetaFloor\dB\ at $q\HeldNoBetaQp$. That is above the budget, so no
allocation on that set meets $0.1\dB$ and the bisection has nothing to return.
The shipped table has a hole where the highest rate should be, and a decoder
holding it falls back to the deepest allocation, which is our own full-depth
path and costs slightly more than the release, so it saves nothing. The test
frames, whose floor at that rate is \HeldFloorTestHigh\dB, would have supported
\HeldNoBetaForgone\ points. What fails there is the calibration set rather than
the router: a budget written as an absolute decibel sits a different distance
above the floor on $512$px photographs than on $1080$p video, and at the highest
rate it sits below it.

We keep the test-bisected figures as B's headline, since the comparison against
A is built on them, and Table~\ref{tab:betaheldout} is the correction a reader
should apply. Calibrating on frames whose tiling penalty matches the ones the
decoder will meet is the fix, and for a video decoder that means calibrating on
video.


\textbf{Retraining with the mask fixed raises agreement and does not simply
raise the saving.} The head above was trained against a suppression term sitting
above its own logits (below). We retrained it with the mask fixed, same recipe
and same $\lambda$. Held-out agreement rises from \RetrainAgreeOld\ to
\RetrainAgreeNew, and the deployed saving moves by $+\RetrainGain$ points at
$q\RetrainGainQp$ and $-\RetrainLoss$ at $q\RetrainLossQp$. We find the retrained head
ahead where the required $\beta$ is small and behind where it is large, which is
the same axis the gap runs along. That is the second time in this paper that
agreement with the oracle has moved opposite to the quantity that matters. We
keep the original head for every other measurement so the comparisons stay on
one system, and we read the retrain as evidence that the mask cost the head real
capacity, and that agreement is not the objective.

An earlier version of this measurement put the gap at $1.7$ points at $q0$,
rising to $13.3$ at $q63$. The exit mask was at fault. It suppresses exits below
the split depth by assigning $-10^{4}$, the head's own logits had drifted to
that scale, and the suppressed entries were therefore the largest in every row.
A large share of every tile went to the cheapest exit for a reason unrelated to
its content. The mask is now $-\infty$. Fixing it costs $3.5$ points at $q0$,
where the accident happened to agree with the oracle, and buys $9.4$ at $q63$,
where it did not.

\subsection{What each router input is worth}

The head reads four per-tile signals and the quality index, and one of them
carries almost all of it. We retrain the same head once per input group, zeroing
the others after their projection rather than deleting them, so architecture,
parameter count, optimiser, seed and data order are identical across the six
runs and only what the head is allowed to know differs. The quality index stays
live everywhere: it is one number per frame and cannot tell two tiles of a frame
apart, so the run with it alone is the floor that no per-tile information
reaches, \InputQpAgree\ agreement.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/router_inputs}}
\caption{\textbf{What each router input is worth.} Agreement with the search's
exit choice on held-out frames. Read the first column against the last: only the
stem moves agreement away from what a single constant exit already achieves.}
\label{tab:routerinputs}
\end{table}

The stem alone reaches \InputStemAgree (Table~\ref{tab:routerinputs}), \InputStemOver\ over the floor, and
adding the latent, the scales and the bit count on top of it reaches
\InputAllAgree, which is not an improvement. The signals are not independent:
the entropy model's scales and the bits spent are both functions of the same
latent the stem was computed from, so the head is being given one piece of
information in four dressings. That is worth stating beside
Section~\ref{sec:raterank}, where a rule reading the bit count alone beats the
whole head: the bit count is not a weak input, it is the same input, read by
something that does not have to learn what to do with it.

\subsection{A router with no parameters}
\label{sec:raterank}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/raterank.png}
\caption{\textbf{The calibrated bit rule.} \textbf{a} Saving at $0.1\dB$; shaded where
the calibrated bit rule beats the trained head. \textbf{b} What a tile's bit
count is correlated with, against how often the rule agrees with the oracle
outright; dotted is the head's own held-out agreement.}
\label{fig:raterank}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/raterank}}
\caption{\textbf{The calibrated bit rule}, $0.1\dB$, same test set; it is the
``rate-rank'' column. Bold where the rule beats the trained head. $\rho$ are
Spearman correlations
between a tile's bit count and, respectively, the depth the oracle assigns it and
the distortion it stands to gain from that depth.}
\label{tab:raterank}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/raterank_best}}
\caption{\textbf{The same comparison on a second training run} (\texttt{BEST}),
$0.1\dB$, same test set. Bold where the calibrated bit rule beats that run's own
trained head.}
\label{tab:raterankbest}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/blend}}
\caption{\textbf{Blending the two decoder-side signals} at $0.1\dB$, both
normalised to unit mean, weight $w$ from the calibrated bit rule to the head's ordering.
Bold is the best per rate.}
\label{tab:blend}
\end{table}

Before a $\RouterParams$ head is worth its \RouterCostPct\% of the decode, it has
to beat what the decoder already knows (Fig.~\ref{fig:raterank}) and Table~\ref{tab:raterank} The shaded region in panel~a is where the free rule is ahead, and it covers
every rate. The entropy model has produced one
number per tile before the trunk runs, and at no cost: how many bits that tile's
latents took.

We turn it into a routing rule with no learned parameters. We model the
per-tile distortion as rank-1 in the log domain,
$\log D(t,k)\approx\alpha\log b(t)+c+\log\varphi_k$, where $b$ is the tile's bit
count normalised by the frame mean and $\varphi$ is a $K$-vector saying what each
exit costs on an average tile. We fit $(\alpha,c,\varphi)$ by least squares,
leave-one-sequence-out, so that no sequence contributes to the profile that
routes it. The same Lagrangian the oracle runs is then run on the surrogate.
Nothing is signalled and nothing is trained; the arithmetic is one scalar per
tile. \textbf{It beats the trained head at every rate.} The calibrated bit rule is ahead
of the \RouterParams\ router at all \RateRankNWins\ measured rates, by margins
that run from half a point at $q48$ to \RateRankBeatsBy\ points at $q0$. A head
trained on this decoder against this oracle therefore returns nothing over a
rule with no parameters at all, and it carries \RouterCostPct\% of the decode
that the calibrated bit rule does not.

\textbf{Why it works is not that it agrees with the oracle.} It agrees on
\RateRankAgreeLo--\RateRankAgreeHi\ of tiles, well below the router's $0.718$,
and still saves more at every rate. Agreement weighs a disagreement on
a tile where two exits are within a hair of each other exactly as heavily as one
where the choice is most of the frame's error, and most tiles are the former.
The ordering is what the rule gets right. Bits correlate with the \emph{spread}
across the ladder, that is, with how much a tile stands to gain from depth, at
$\rho_{\mathrm{spread}}=\RateRankSpreadLo$--\RateRankSpreadHi\ at every rate.

\textbf{At a looser budget it stops being a baseline and becomes the answer.}
At $0.3\dB$ the calibrated bit rule matches the oracle exactly at the three lowest
rates, where both reach the same architectural ceiling, comes within $0.2$
points of it at $q48$, and gives up \RateRankLoose\% against the oracle's
\SigLooseHigh\% at $q63$. That is ahead of the trained head at every rate, by up to
\RateRankLooseAheadBy\ points. The head is charged for itself and the rule
is not. At a loose budget the head's ordering also has less left to contribute,
because once the budget saturates the ladder there is little ordering left to
get right, and the rule gets it. At $0.5\dB$ it reaches the ceiling at
\RateRankHalfDbExact\ rate and its assignment is \emph{identical} to the
oracle's on every tile. \textbf{What it cannot do} is see
anything beyond that ordering. A rank-1 model in the level assigns every tile the
same relative profile over exits, so $b$ only decides where on the ladder a tile
falls, never the shape of its trade-off. That is the ceiling this baseline sits
at, and it is the part a learned head should be earning its parameters on. Ours
does not earn them at any rate we measured.

\textbf{It replicates on a second training run.}
\texttt{BEST} is a separate recipe at a different epoch, with its own router
trained the same way. There the calibrated bit rule beats the trained head at
\BestRankWinsN\ of \BestRankOfN\ rates, by up to \BestRankBy\ points, and comes
within \BestRankToOracle\ points of the \emph{oracle} everywhere
(Table~\ref{tab:raterankbest}). The margins there are wider than here, and the
one rate it concedes is the only rate on either checkpoint where the head
finishes ahead, by under a point. We do not read that as showing a learned head
cannot be worth its parameters, only that neither of our training runs produced
one that is. The calibrated bit rule stays close to the oracle on both.

Per-block bit allocation is a standard quantity in learned compression, where it
is something to \emph{choose}; block-level rate control sets it so that complex
regions get more bits~\cite{blockratecontrol}. We read the same number in the
other direction, after the fact and at the decoder, as a statement about how hard
a region was. It costs nothing because someone else has already paid for it.

\textbf{Are the two signals complementary?} Barely. We normalise both surrogates
to unit mean and blend them with one weight $w$, where $w{=}0$ is the
calibrated bit rule and $w{=}1$ the head's ordering. The best blend is $w{=}0$ at
the three lowest rates and a small head weight at the two highest, worth \BlendGainMid\ points at \BlendGainMidQ\ and \BlendGainHigh\ at \BlendGainHighQ (Table~\ref{tab:blend}). The head reads the
entropy model's scales, so it already has most of what the bit count carries; what it adds is confined to \BlendGainMidQ\ and \BlendGainHighQ.

\paragraph{How much a trained head varies, and what that does to the claim.} No
head here was trained twice at two seeds, so we have no seed variance to report.
What we can report is the spread between two heads trained independently on the
same decoder, which is looser than seed variance and larger. The joint and the
frozen head differ by \HeadSpreadLow\ points at the lowest rate and
\HeadSpreadHigh\ at the highest, a range of \HeadSpreadRange\ points, and they cross: whichever is better depends on the rate. Both are read off the arithmetic model rather than the hook count,
because only one of them was hook-counted, and mixing the two conventions
adds most of a point to the spread. At \HeadSpreadWiderN\ of the \HeadSpreadRatesN\ rates that spread is wider
than the rule's margin over whichever head is nearer. So the claim we make is not
that no learned router can beat the bit rule. It is that a rule costing nothing
sits inside the band two of our own trained heads span, which is where a control
belongs.

A learned component should be measured against the free alternative, and it
rarely is. In adaptive inference the usual controls are a uniform allocation and
a random one. Both are much weaker than a decoder-side signal that is already
lying around (Fig.~\ref{fig:deciders}). Panel~b of that figure is the surprise: the rule picks the search's exit on
fewer than half the tiles and still captures three quarters of its saving, which
is why agreement is the wrong thing to optimise.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/deciders.png}
\caption{\textbf{Three ways to choose an exit.} \textbf{a}, saving at $0.1\dB$. The
encoder search sees the source and sends \MapBits\ bits a frame; the other two
send nothing. The bit rule beats the trained head at every rate, with no learned
parameters against the head's \RouterParams. \textbf{b}, bars are the tiles where
the rule picks the search's exit, the line the fraction of its saving it captures
anyway.}
\label{fig:deciders}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Signalling only what the router gets wrong}
\label{sec:hybrid}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/hybrid.png}
\caption{\textbf{Partial signalling.} \textbf{a}, saving against the bits spent on the map;
each line runs from B on the left to A on the right. \textbf{b}, the same
normalised by the A-to-B gap; dashed is proportional recovery. \textbf{c},
against the fixed-$\lambda$ Lorenz bound; points above the dashed line are
allocations one multiplier cannot reach.}
\label{fig:hybrid}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/hybrid}}
\caption{\textbf{Configuration C} at $0.1\dB$. Columns are the fraction of tiles
the encoder overrides; the two end columns reproduce B and A to within
$0.1$ points, which is the check that the interpolation is real.}
\label{tab:hybrid}
\end{table}

The encoder knows tile by tile where the router will be wrong, because it can run
that router itself (Section~\ref{sec:setting}), and nothing obliges it to correct
every one of them. That is the room configuration C works in (Fig.~\ref{fig:hybrid}) and Table~\ref{tab:hybrid} The curves in panel~a rise steeply and then flatten: almost all of what
signalling buys is bought by the first tenth of the tiles.

We choose the $\rho N$ overridden tiles by Lagrangian regret,
$\Delta(t)=L_\lambda(t,\hat{k}_t)-L_\lambda(t,k^{*}_t)$, where
$L_\lambda(t,k) = D_{t,k}+\lambda c_k$ is the objective
of~(\ref{eq:lagrangian}), so $\Delta(t)$ is exactly what that objective loses on
tile $t$ by staying silent. We hold $\beta$ at B's value and bisect $\lambda$
over the overrides to land back on the budget. The map costs an entropy-coded
mask, $N H_2(\rho)$ bits with $H_2$ the binary entropy, plus $3$ per override.
\textbf{The two ends check out.} At $\rho{=}0$ the sweep reproduces configuration~B
and at $\rho{=}1$ it reproduces~A, each to within
\HybridEndOffsetLo--\HybridEndOffsetHi\ points. That residue is not
disagreement: this sweep was never hook-counted, so its savings come from the
arithmetic model, and the model over-reports by exactly that much (Section~\ref{sec:exp}). Neither end is imposed; both fall out of the same code path run
against independently measured files, so the columns between them are measuring
something real.

\textbf{Most of the gap is cheap.} Overriding a tenth of the tiles for
\HybridBitsTenth\ bits per frame recovers
\HybridRecoverTenthLow--\HybridRecoverTenthHigh\% of the gap, and a fifth
recovers \HybridRecoverFifthLow--\HybridRecoverFifthHigh\%. Recovery is concave
everywhere, so the first bits spent are the most useful ones.

\textbf{And a partial map can beat a complete one.} At \HybridBeatsAN\ of
\HybridBeatsAOf\ rates, signalling half the tiles for \HybridBitsHalf\ bits
saves \emph{more} than signalling all of them, by up to \HybridBeatsABy\ points,
at the same distortion. Both land within the bisection's $5\times10^{-4}\dB$
tolerance of the budget, and the local exchange rate is about $48$ saving points
per decibel, so the tolerance is worth $0.02$ points against a margin ten to
twenty times that. The margin is therefore real, and it does not come from a
better predictor. The hybrid has \emph{two} multipliers where A has one: the
oracle's $\lambda$ governs the overridden tiles and the router's fixed $\beta$
the rest. A two-multiplier allocation reaches points on the distortion--compute
plane that a single Lagrangian sweep cannot, for the same reason the sweep
misses interior Pareto points at all (Section~\ref{sec:operating}).
Configuration~A is optimal among allocations reachable by one multiplier, and
that is a smaller set than the word suggests.

\textbf{Why the recovery is concave, and what bounds it.} At a fixed $\lambda$
the objective is separable, so overriding a set removes \emph{exactly} the sum
of that set's regrets. The recovery of the \emph{objective} is then the Lorenz
curve of the per-tile regret distribution, and its curvature is that
distribution's Gini coefficient, \GiniMin--\GiniMax\ across rates. What the
table reports is saving at fixed distortion, not the objective, and returning to
the budget means re-bisecting $\lambda$. That re-bisection is also what lets the
two-multiplier allocations above escape the bound.

\textbf{At the loose budget it matters where the gap is.} At $0.3\dB$ the three
lowest rates are saturated, and there is nothing for a partial map to buy. At
\HybridLooseQps, where the gap is \GapLooseHigh\ points, half the map recovers
\HybridLooseRecLo--\HybridLooseRecHi\% of it. The allocation follows the same
rule here as everywhere else, which is to spend the bits where the ladder still
has somewhere to go.

\textbf{A better predictor concentrates its regret, which is what the Gini was
for.} We rebuild C on the retrained head of Section~\ref{sec:ab}. The Gini of the
per-tile regret rises at \GiniRetrainUpN\ of \GiniRetrainOfN\ rates, to
\GiniRetrainLo--\GiniRetrainHi. Its mistakes are rarer and larger. The same
table shows the consequence. C converges on A faster from a better base and has
less left to recover, and the half-beats-all effect disappears at $q0$, because
a base close to A leaves little for the extra multiplier to exploit. The Lorenz
reading is therefore worth having as a diagnostic and not as a decoration; it
reports what \emph{kind} of predictor one has as well as how good it is.

\textbf{Which predictor should C be built on?} Either will do, and the answer
follows the same split as Section~\ref{sec:raterank}. Running the identical
override rule over the calibrated bit rule instead of the head is worth up
to \CPredBitsAhead\ points at the lowest rate and costs up to \CPredHeadAhead\
at the highest. Both converge on A at $\rho{=}1$ to the second decimal at every
rate, which is the third independent check that the two code paths agree. The
best single operating point we measured is the calibrated bit rule with half the map
signalled, at \CBestSave\% at $q\CBestQp$. That is \CBestOverA\ points
\emph{above} full signalling, with no learned component anywhere in the decoder.

Configuration C is what we would ship where a small map is tolerable and a large
one is not. It also reframes the A--B gap. What the gap measures is the price of
\emph{silence}, charged tile by tile, rather than the price of prediction.
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/concentration.png}
\caption{\textbf{The loss is concentrated.} \textbf{a}, the share of the total regret carried by the worst fraction of tiles, per rate; the dotted line is an even spread. \textbf{b}, the same as a Gini coefficient.}
\label{fig:concentration}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Does the map have to be recomputed?}
\label{sec:transfer}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/map_transfer.png}
\caption{\textbf{Reusing an exit map.} Solid is the transferred map, dashed the
one recomputed in place. \textbf{a}, \textbf{b}: reuse across frames of the same
sequence. \textbf{c}: reuse across quality index; the entry is the delivered
distortion against a $0.1\dB$ budget.}
\label{fig:transfer}
\end{figure}

How much A's extra decode at the encoder matters depends on how often the map has
to be recomputed (Fig.~\ref{fig:transfer}) Panel~c reads as a matrix of what a map costs when it is applied at a rate it
was not computed for. It is markedly asymmetric., and we have not seen that measured anywhere.

\textbf{Across frames.} Reuse is close to free. We take the map found on frame
$0$ and apply it eight frames later; at $q0$ the delivered distortion rises by
\TransferDbCost$\dB$, five percent of the budget, and the saving does not move
at all: \TransferSaving\% transferred against
\TransferInPlaceLo--\TransferInPlaceHi\% recomputed. The allocation is a
property of where the content is hard, and that moves slowly. A codec would
search once per group of pictures instead of once per frame, and divide the
encoder cost by the group length.

\textbf{Across rate.} Here the map does have to be recomputed, and the direction
of the reuse decides how badly. Found at $q0$ and applied at $q63$, it delivers
\TransferCrossDb$\dB$ against a $0.1\dB$ budget, claiming the low-rate saving of
\TransferSaving\% while spending nearly twice the quality it is allowed. The
reverse is safe but wasteful: the $q63$ map applied at $q0$ delivers $0.075\dB$
and only $19.8\%$ where \ClassLowUvg\% was available. Shallow exits are cheap in
quality at low rate and expensive at high rate, so a map is calibrated to the
rate it was found at, and reusing one upward breaks the quality guarantee
without anything in the decode reporting that it has. In our reuse probe, then, an encoder can search once per rate and reuse that
search across the frames we tested. How far that carries beyond the offsets and
sequences probed here we have not measured.

\subsection{What the frame mean is made of}

The budget binds on a frame, and a frame is 40 tiles. At the $0.1\dB$ budget the
median tile of the lowest rate gives up \TailMedian\dB, which is about what the
frame gives up, but the ninety-ninth percentile is \TailPNinetyNine\dB and the worst
single tile in \TailNTiles\ is \TailMax. \TailOverOne\ tiles lose more than a
decibel while their frames stay inside a tenth of one
(Table~\ref{tab:tiletail}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/tiletail}
\caption{\textbf{The distribution behind the frame mean.} Per-tile loss against
the released decoder at the $0.1\dB$ budget, over every tile of every test
sequence.}
\label{tab:tiletail}
\end{table}

Which tiles they are is the part that matters, and it is the seam of
Section~\ref{sec:seam} arriving in the allocation. Split the tiles by whether
their receptive field reaches an invented value: the interior tiles give up
\TailInterior\dB on average and the \TailBorderN\ tiles with padding give up
\TailBorder, \TailBorderRatio\ times as much. The border is not only where the
picture is damaged, it is where the allocation is most expensive, because a tile
that already carries a seam has less room left inside the budget before it has to
decode deeper. A deployment that wants a per-tile guarantee rather than a
per-frame one has a straightforward lever: clamp the shallowest exit a border
tile may take, at the cost of the saving those tiles carry.

The tail also has a depth. Split the same tiles by the exit they took and the
whole of it sits at the shallowest rung: tiles at \TailExitLo\ lose
\TailExitLoMean\dB on average and \TailExitLoOver\ of them lose more than half
a decibel, while every tile at a deeper exit averages \TailExitRestMean\dB and
\TailExitRestOver\ of them pass half a decibel. The multiplier is doing what it
was asked to do, spending the budget where it is cheapest, and the consequence is
that the loss is not spread thinly over the frame but concentrated on the tiles
it sent furthest. That is the same concentration Section~\ref{sec:ab} uses to
build configuration~C, seen from the distortion side rather than the regret
side.

\subsection{A budget in one metric is not a budget in another}

Every allocation in this paper is bisected on PSNR, which prices a squared error
and nothing else. The obvious question is what that does to a metric built to
track perception, so we measure MS-SSIM on the same frames at the same operating
point (Table~\ref{tab:msssim}), converted to decibels by $-10\log_{10}(1-m)$ so
the two are read on one scale.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/msssim}
\caption{\textbf{Two metrics at one operating point.} The $0.1\dB$ budget,
\NumSeq\ sequences, configuration~A. MS-SSIM is converted to decibels by
$-10\log_{10}(1-m)$. Both columns are what the routed decode gives up against
the released decoder on the same latent.}
\label{tab:msssim}
\end{table}

The perceptual metric loses less than the budget spends. Against \MsPsnrLoss\dB
of PSNR the same decodes give up \MsSsimLossLo--\MsSsimLossHi\dB of MS-SSIM,
\MsSsimRatio\ of the PSNR loss, at every rate. We do not read that as a
perceptual claim. The shallow exits blur, and blurring costs a squared error more
than it costs a structural similarity, so a budget written in PSNR is the
conservative one of the two to write. What it is not is evenly priced across
content: the sequence that gives up most MS-SSIM is \MsWorstSeq, which loses
\MsWorstDb\ of it while saving \MsWorstSaving\% of the arithmetic, and it is
an ordinary 1080p clip from the middle of the set rather than one of the hard
cases. A deployment that cares about a particular metric should bisect on that
metric; nothing in the method depends on which one it is.

\subsection{Complexity and wall-clock}
\label{sec:wallclock}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/complexity}
\caption{\textbf{Decoder complexity} at 1080p. Our deepest exit costs slightly
more than the released decoder because it still pays the deblocking filter; that
$1.0095$, not $1.0$, is what every saving in this paper is \emph{not} divided by.
Wall-clock is the sorted loop of Section~\ref{sec:wallclock}.}
\label{tab:complexity}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/latency}
\caption{\textbf{Wall-clock}, 1080p, median of 40 interleaved iterations on one
NVIDIA RTX A6000 with a $300$\,W board limit, PyTorch $2.6.0$ and CUDA $12.4$, single precision, one frame per iteration after $20$ warm-up iterations, at the $0.1\dB$ operating point. ``MACs'' is what the arithmetic
predicts; ``measured'' is the sorted per-tile loop of
Section~\ref{sec:wallclock}.}
\label{tab:latency}
\end{table}

A saving in multiply--accumulates is not a saving in time (Table~\ref{tab:complexity}). Tiling costs
\TilingOverhead\% before anything exits early, measured as the deepest-exit
tiled decode against the released full-frame one at the same arithmetic and the
same weights. On top of that, the routed decode realises \WallSorted\% at q0 where its operations predict
\WallPredicted\%, and \WallHighMeasured\% at q63 against
\WallHighPredicted\%: about four fifths of the predicted saving arrives at
either end. What does not arrive is the tiling overhead together with the
bookkeeping of a shrinking active set, and a MAC count sees neither. The
shortfall scales with the saving rather than sitting at a fixed offset,
\WallShortLow\ points at the low rate against \WallShortHigh\ at the high
one. Both figures are the sorted loop; written as the obvious one the
low-rate decode realises \WallMasked\%, which is where the
\WallSortedGain\ points below come from.

\paragraph{Seconds and joules.} Multiply-accumulates are the right unit to
optimise, because they do not depend on the machine, but they are not the unit a
deployment cares about. We measured both on the padded 1080p frame, sampling
board power from the driver at $100$\,ms and running each condition for a fixed
wall time rather than a fixed iteration count, because the sensor updates too
slowly for ten iterations of a $100$\,ms decode to mean anything. Idle power was
measured before and after each condition so that a neighbouring process waking up
would appear as drift rather than as a saving.

Energy follows time, not arithmetic (Fig.~\ref{fig:power}). At $q0$, $q32$ and $q63$ the routed decode
removes \PowerMacLow, \PowerMacMid\ and \PowerMacHigh\% of the arithmetic; it removes \PowerTimeLow, \PowerTimeMid
and \PowerTimeHigh\% of the wall clock and \PowerEnergyLow, \PowerEnergyMid\ and \PowerEnergyHigh\% of the joules per
frame. Board power barely moves, $298$\,W against $296$\,W at $q0$, because the
later groups run on a shrinking set of tiles and a partly idle GPU still draws
most of its static power. What early exit buys is a shorter decode, not a cooler
one. Frame rate at 1080p goes from \FpsFull\ to \FpsRouted, and peak memory rises by
\PeakDelta\% at every resolution we could measure: tiling turns one feature map into
a batch of small ones, so the peak is set by the widest point of the ladder
rather than by its deepest.

Sorting the tiles once by exit depth recovers part of it. The obvious
implementation of a shrinking active set keeps a boolean mask, gathers the
survivors and scatters the finished at every group boundary, and each of those
boundaries forces a device-to-host synchronisation. Order the tiles by
descending exit depth and ``still active at group $g$'' becomes a contiguous
prefix: each group is then a slice instead of a gather, and one cumulative count
supplies every boundary, so no per-group mask is built at all. The finished
tiles come back through the inverse permutation in a single scatter. The
arithmetic is unchanged and the output is bit-identical on GPU. At $q0$ the
saving goes from \WallMasked\% to \WallSorted\% (Table~\ref{tab:latency}), a
gain of \WallSortedGain\ points, or a fifth of the shortfall, for a change that
touches no arithmetic.

The same gap appears in our own accounting. The router is charged at its share of
the decoder's multiply--accumulates, \RouterCostPct\%
(Section~\ref{sec:setting}). We also timed the head directly, on the padded
$2048{\times}1280$ frame the decoder actually sees, interleaved against a
deepest-exit decode so that a co-tenant's load falls on both equally. It costs
\RouterTimePct\%, which is \RouterTimeFactor$\times$ what its arithmetic
predicts, and for the same reason as everything else in this section: a
\RouterParams-parameter head is launch overhead, and a MAC count cannot see a
launch. Charged at measured time instead of at operations, every B number in
this paper would fall by a further \RouterTimeExtra\ points. We leave them
charged at MACs because that is the convention the rest of the literature
reports in, and we record the correction here so that it does not sit unstated.

A paper that quotes only operations would report \WallPredicted\% where the same
code, run as written, delivers \WallSorted\%. That is why we give the shortfall
as well. The error runs one way: operations are an \emph{optimistic} bound on
this method, and the optimism grows with how much of the frame exits early.

\subsection{Where the saving is realised, and where it is not}

That optimism is a scheduling cost, and scheduling belongs to the device rather
than to the method: the last groups of the trunk run on a handful of tiles and
the card is largely idle waiting for them. If that is what the gap is, a machine
that does not care how many tiles are in flight should not show it. We measured
the same decodes on a CPU with \CpuThreads\ threads, and at three batch sizes on
the GPU to see whether feeding it more work closes the gap instead
(Table~\ref{tab:cpubatch}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/cpu_batch}
\caption{\textbf{The same saving in three places.} Per cent removed at the
$0.1\dB$ budget on a padded 1080p frame: the arithmetic model, the GPU at two
batch sizes, and the CPU. Arithmetic is the same in every column; only the
machine changes.}
\label{tab:cpubatch}
\end{table}

On the CPU the bound is not optimistic. At the lowest rate the routed decode
takes \CpuMsRouted\ seconds against \CpuMsStock, which is \CpuSavingLow\%
removed where the arithmetic model predicts \CpuPredLow\%. It realises slightly
more than the operations count, because the tiles that exit early stop touching
memory as well as arithmetic, and nothing there is waiting on a wide device to
fill. The GPU recovers \BatchGainLow\ points by batching, and stops
there. At the highest rate the CPU falls back to \CpuSavingHigh\%, in line with
the GPU, because at that rate the allocation is deep and there is little left to
skip. The claim we take from this is narrow: the gap between operations and time
is a scheduling property of the accelerator, and on a device without one the
operations count is the honest figure.

\subsection{The right ladder depends on the budget}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/ladder_crossover.png}
\caption{\textbf{The right ladder depends on the budget.} Saving against budget
for four ladders, with each one's architectural ceiling as a dotted line. A finer
ladder has a higher ceiling and a higher floor, so the curves cross: the coarse
ladder wins where the budget is tight and cannot be spent, and the fine one wins
where it is loose enough to reach exits the coarse ladder does not have.}
\label{fig:laddercross}
\end{figure}

\label{sec:ladder}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/runs}}
\caption{\textbf{Ladder settings}, mean saving (\%) over the five rates, on
each run's own latest checkpoint. Ceilings are $100(1-c_j)$ for that ladder,
corrected by the offset the hook count shows. $^{\ast}$ some rate did not reach
the budget. $^{\dagger}$ the saving is from the arithmetic model rather than
counted off the decode, and is therefore $0.4$--$0.8$ points optimistic; only
RECIPE512 has been re-measured with hooks at every budget.}
\label{tab:runs}
\end{table}

Section~\ref{sec:operating} argued that once a budget saturates a ladder, the
only way to spend more is an exit that does not exist. Table~\ref{tab:runs}
measures that. A finer ladder ($K{=}12$, $j{=}4$) has a higher ceiling than the
shipped one's \Ceiling\%, and the two orderings cross somewhere between $0.1$
and $0.3\dB$:

\begin{itemize}\itemsep1pt
\item At $0.1\dB$ the coarse ladder wins, and the fine one cannot even reach the
      budget at the highest rate. Splitting later ($j{=}4$ against $j{=}2$) puts
      twice as many blocks in the per-tile section, which by
      Eq.~(\ref{eq:contam}) raises the floor.
\item At $0.5\dB$ the fine ladder wins by \FineHalfGain\ points, \FineHalfDb\% against
      \CoarseHalfDb\%, because the coarse one has been pinned at its ceiling
      since $0.3\dB$ and has nothing left to spend.
\end{itemize}

So the ladder is a choice made at the operating point, not a hyperparameter
tuned once and fixed. The band of Section~\ref{sec:operating} tells you which
side of the crossover a given budget sits on (Fig.~\ref{fig:laddercross}) The two dotted lines in that figure are the two ceilings, and the crossing
between them is the whole argument: a finer ladder is worse until the budget is
large enough to reach past the coarse one's ceiling..

\section{Against the released decoder}
\label{sec:released}

Everything above is measured against the released DCVC-UF intra decoder, but
always as a percentage. This section states it once in the units a codec paper
reports, so the comparison can be read without arithmetic.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/qualitative.png}
\caption{\textbf{What \QualSaving\% of the arithmetic costs, to look at.}
\QualSeq\ at q\QualQp, one frame, with $\lambda$ bisected on that frame to
\QualDb\dB. Both crops are decoded from the \emph{same} latent at \QualBpp\ bpp:
the released decoder reaches \QualPsnrRel\dB and the routed decode
\QualPsnrOurs\dB. The crop is centred on the tile that gave up the most, tile
\QualWorstTile\ of \QualNTiles, not on a flattering one. Right, the absolute
difference at $\times$\QualAmp.}
\label{fig:qualitative}
\end{figure}

The difference panel is the part worth reading (Fig.~\ref{fig:qualitative}). Amplified twenty times, what it
shows is the rigging of the boat, the waterline and the edge of the flag, and
almost nothing along the tile borders that cross the crop. The error the budget
permits is spent where the picture is difficult, which is where the shallow
exits fail, and not at the seams that Section~\ref{sec:seam} spends its length
on. That is the seam repair and the border padding doing their work: the cut is
still the largest single cost in the method, and by the time the reader sees the
picture it is no longer the visible one.

The same frame at the top of the rate range says what the budget costs there (Fig.~\ref{fig:qualitativehigh}). At
$q\QualHighQp$, \QualHighBpp\ bpp, the released decoder reaches
\QualHighPsnrRel\dB and the routed decode \QualHighPsnrOurs\dB for
\QualHighDb\dB delivered, and the saving is \QualHighSaving\% against
\QualSaving\% at $q\QualQp$. The allocation is what moved: on this frame
\QualShallowLow\ of 40 tiles take the shallowest exit at $q\QualQp$ and
\QualShallowHigh\ does at $q\QualHighQp$, while the deepest exit goes from
\QualDeepLow\ tiles to \QualDeepHigh. The picture is as hard to tell apart at
either rate. What changes is how much of the decoder the budget will release,
which is the rate dependence of Section~\ref{sec:operating} arriving in a single
frame.

\QualHighPsnrRel\dB and the routed decode \QualHighPsnrOurs\dB, for

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/released}}
\caption{\textbf{FLEX-UF against the decoder it modifies.} The released DCVC-UF
intra decoder and the same decoder with the exit ladder, at the three budgets.
Arithmetic is counted with hooks on the executed decode. ``dB below release'' is

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/power.png}
\caption{\textbf{Three units for one saving.} \textbf{a}, the same routed decode
measured as arithmetic, as wall clock and as joules per frame, at 1080p and a

the board draws the same power either way, because the later groups run on a

\label{fig:power}
\end{figure}

The released decoder spends \RelGmac\ GMAC on a padded 1080p frame (Table~\ref{tab:released}), which is
\RelKMacPx\ thousand multiply-accumulates for every pixel it produces, and it
spends the same on every pixel whatever the picture is doing there. At a
$0.1\dB$ budget the ladder takes that to \GmacAtOne\ GMAC, \KmacAtOne\ kMAC per
pixel, and delivers \DbAtOne\dB\ below the release for a BD-Rate cost of
\BdRateALow\%.

The $0.3$ and $0.5\dB$ rows are the same measurement with the constraint
loosened, and they say something the percentages hide. Between them the saving
moves by less than a point, from \MeanAtThree\% to \MeanAtFive\%, while the
budget grows by two thirds. The ladder has run out of exits: at $0.3\dB$ most
tiles are already on the cheapest rung they are allowed and the extra allowance
buys nothing. The delivered distortion says the same, \DbAtThree\dB\ against a
$0.3\dB$ allowance. A looser budget is not the way to get more out of this
decoder; a finer ladder is, and Section~\ref{sec:exp} measures one.

In wall clock on one RTX A6000, at \PowerQMid\ and the $0.1\dB$ budget, a
padded 1080p frame decodes in \PowerMsMid\ ms against the release's
\PowerMsFullMid, which is \PowerFpsFullMid\ frames per second becoming
\PowerFpsMid, and it does so for \PowerJMid\ J against \PowerJFullMid. The
arithmetic saving is \PowerMacMid\% at that rate and the energy saving is
\PowerEnergyMid\%, and the gap between those two numbers is the scheduling
cost of a decode that runs its last groups on a handful of tiles.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\input{tables/bdrate}
\caption{\textbf{BD-Rate against the released decoder}, integrated over the five
quality indices, and what each configuration puts in the file to get it.}
\label{tab:bdrate}
\end{table}

BD-Rate is the number a codec paper is read on, so we give it for both
configurations at all three budgets rather than only for the headline
(Table~\ref{tab:bdrate}). Two things in the table are worth reading against each
other. The cost of a budget is not linear in it: going from $0.1$ to $0.3\dB$
nearly triples the BD-Rate while the saving moves by \GapBudgetPoints\ points,
because the second decibel is spent on tiles that were already cheap. And B pays
marginally less than A at every budget, which is not B being better: it delivers
slightly less saving for slightly less distortion, and it sends nothing, so the
\MapBits\ bits A spends are the whole of the difference in what reaches the
file.

\section{Limitations}
That result is bounded on four sides: by a cost the method pays and cannot
yet remove, by the kind of frame it was measured on, by where in its training
the measured model sits, and by the fact that there is one of it. We take them
in that order.

\label{sec:limits}

\paragraph{The seam is reduced, and the exact remedy is not usable as it stands.}
The halo exchange removes \CoupFloorDropLo--\CoupFloorDropHi\% of the floor and
is bit-exact at uniform depth (Section~\ref{sec:coupling}). On a decoder trained
with independent-tile padding, introducing the exchange only at inference also
destroys the routed saving, because routing puts neighbouring tiles at different
depths and the exchange then carries a shallow tile's feature into a deep
neighbour. We state it that way deliberately: the finding is about this decoder
and this training, not about halo exchange in general. We do
not know whether a decoder trained with the exchange can recover both at once, and
that is the experiment we would run next. Until someone runs it, the floor is a
cost this method pays.

\paragraph{Intra frames only.} This is the image path of a video codec.
Extending the ladder to inter frames raises a question we do not answer here,
because an exit map propagates through the reference chain and a shallow tile in
one frame is a worse reference for the next one.

\paragraph{The checkpoint is early in its schedule.} Every number in this paper
is measured on one pinned checkpoint, \texttt{runs/RECIPE512/ckpt\_PAPER.pth.tar},
taken at the end of the first pass over the training set. It is pinned because a
moving checkpoint was overwritten mid-measurement once, and a paper whose tables
come from three different epochs is worse than one whose tables are early. Later
checkpoints of the same run improved the measured trade-off, and monotonically:
on the same \NumSeq\ frames at the same budget, with the same hook count, the run
reads \EpochMeanZero\%, \EpochMeanOne\%, \EpochMeanTwo\% and \EpochMeanThree\% at
epochs $0$ to \EpochLatest, a gain of \EpochGain\ points over the checkpoint this
paper reports, and it was still training when we stopped measuring. We report the
pinned checkpoint because every table has to come from one set of weights, and we
do not read \EpochGain\ points as a bound on what a converged run would give.


\paragraph{A single decoder.} All results are on DCVC-UF's intra decoder. Nothing
in the method looks specific to it, since the ladder needs only a residual trunk
with a shared head, but we have not measured a second decoder to check.

\paragraph{Beyond those four, seven mechanisms are not in the system, and each
was removed by a measurement rather than by taste.} The supplement tabulates all
seven with the number that ended each. Five were built and dropped, one is an extension the
measurement did not support, and the last is an explanation of the tiling
penalty that does not predict it. We report them because what fails is the part
most likely to transfer: the border
estimators say the seam is not an interpolation problem, the halo exchange says
exactness and adaptivity are in tension, and the frozen trunk says the ladder
has to be trained through.


% =========================================================== conclusion
\section{Conclusion}

The intra decoder of DCVC-UF can be run at a depth chosen per tile from its
content. At a $0.1\dB$ budget this removes \MainLowRate\% to \MainHighRate\% of
its multiply--accumulates for a BD-Rate cost of \BdRateALow\%, with no change to
the encoder and none to the payload. Three lessons should carry to decoders of
this class, and none is about early exit.

\textbf{Tiling is the dominant cost and it is governed by depth.} It traces back
to a single $3\times3$ that is $0.29\%$ of the arithmetic, and the penalty grows
as the square of how many run per tile; the affected-area fraction usually
quoted predicts it badly.

\textbf{The exact remedy is in tension with the thing it enables.} Giving each
convolution its real neighbour is bit-identical at uniform depth; under routing
it destroys the allocation, because routing violates the condition that makes it
exact. Any method mixing spatial adaptivity with tiled inference meets this.

\textbf{A distortion budget is only a control variable inside a measurable band.}
Below the floor it admits nothing; above saturation more buys nothing. A saving
quoted without saying where in that band it sits omits what matters.

Three cautions attach. A saving in operations bounds one in time optimistically,
and the optimism scales with it. A learned router needs a free baseline; ours
loses to one costing nothing. And a timing harness reports numbers even when it
times the wrong thing.
